o: Assign all 26 letters to 9 buttons, ≤ 3 letters per button; typing the i-th letter of a button costs i presses. Minimize total presses for string s. Clearly frequent letters should be first on some button (cost 1), next-most-frequent cost 2, etc. Example 1: all letters of "apple" are distinct and frequent, cost 5. Example 2: 12 distinct letters → nine cost 1, three cost 2 → 15.
k: Only letter frequencies matter, not order within s.
Greedy exchange argument: sort frequencies descending; the i-th most frequent letter should cost ⌈(i+1)/9⌉ presses — any swap with a less frequent letter never helps.
Each button holds at most 3 letters, so costs cycle 1,1,...,1 (nine times), then 2 nine times, then 3.

a.i: Count letter frequencies, sort them descending, and assign press-costs round-robin across the 9 buttons: frequency rank r (0-based) costs r // 9 + 1 presses. Summing cost × frequency gives the optimum.
a.t: O(n + 26 log 26) — counting the string plus sorting 26 frequencies.

a.n: Approach 2: Bucket Counting Instead of Comparison Sort
a.i: Since frequencies are bounded by |s| ≤ 1e5, use counting sort: tally how many letters have each frequency, then walk frequencies from high to low assigning costs. This removes the log factor from sorting the 26 counters (negligible here, but a nice variant).
s: Build freq[f] = number of letters occurring exactly f times.
Iterate f from |s| down to 1; for each of freq[f] letters assign the next cost (r // 9 + 1) and accumulate.
a.t: O(n + |s|) — counting pass plus one sweep over possible frequencies.

w: Present the counting-sort greedy; mention the exchange argument to justify correctness. Pitfalls: forgetting the cap of 3 letters per button is automatically handled by the r//9 formula (26 letters ⇒ max cost 3), and Java overflow is impossible here (≤ 1e5 × 3). Follow-up: buttons with different capacities, or minimizing maximum presses per character.
